source_batch.unit_label: Module B unit 3 (part 3): Pillars 2 and 3, capital buffers, leverage ratio, systemically important banks and risk based supervision

facts.statement: Pillar 2 is the supervisory review process (SREP). Its objective is that a bank has adequate capital to support all the risks in its business and is encouraged to develop better risk management; the bank's Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) is an important component, and banks must have a Board approved policy on it. The main aspects: risks not fully captured by the Pillar 1 minimum, risks not taken into account by Pillar 1, and factors external to the bank. Examples of such risks: interest rate risk in the banking book, credit concentration, liquidity, settlement, reputational and strategic risk, underestimation of credit risk under the standardised approach, model risk, weakness in credit risk mitigants and residual securitisation risk. The Basel Committee's four principles: (1) banks should assess overall capital adequacy against their risk profile and have a strategy to maintain capital; (2) supervisors review the banks' assessments and act if unsatisfied; (3) banks should operate above the minimum ratios and supervisors can require more; (4) supervisors should intervene early to prevent capital falling below minimum levels and require rapid remedial action. The ICAAP should be forward looking, risk based, include stress tests and scenario analyses, and be independently reviewed; a bank using models should have documented specifications, back testing, independent validation and stress testing.
facts.locator: Chapter V, paragraphs 220 to 222; S03 printed pp. 345-350, section 13.12

facts.statement: Pillar 3 (market discipline) complements the minimum capital requirements and the supervisory review by requiring disclosures so that market participants can assess the scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment processes and capital adequacy. It applies at the top consolidated level of the banking group; an individual bank discloses on a stand-alone basis when it is not the top consolidated entity. Banks disclose at least half yearly, whether or not the statements are audited, except Table DF-2 (capital adequacy), DF-3 (credit risk general disclosures) and DF-4 (credit risk, standardised approach), which are disclosed at least quarterly; disclosures are in the published results or on the bank's website with a regulatory disclosures section, with an archive of at least three years of templates (courseware); the capital instruments main features template is updated whenever a new instrument is issued or an existing one is redeemed, converted or written down.
facts.locator: Paragraph 247 and the Pillar 3 chapter; S03 printed pp. 350-352, section 13.13

facts.statement: The capital conservation buffer (CCB) is 2.5 per cent of risk-weighted assets in CET1, above the regulatory minimum, designed so that banks build buffers in normal times and draw them down in stress. When a bank's CET1 falls into the buffer range, constraints apply only to distributions (dividends, share buybacks, discretionary payments on other Tier 1 instruments and discretionary staff bonuses), not to its business operations. Minimum capital conservation ratios by CET1 ratio after current retained earnings: 5.5 to 6.125 per cent: 100 per cent of earnings conserved; above 6.125 to 6.75: 80; above 6.75 to 7.375: 60; above 7.375 to 8.0: 40; above 8.0: 0. CET1 is first used to meet the 5.5 per cent CET1, 7 per cent Tier 1 and 9 per cent total capital minima, so a bank with 9 per cent CET1 and no AT1 or Tier 2 capital has a zero buffer and a 100 per cent constraint. A bank with no positive earnings and CET1 below 8 per cent cannot make positive net distributions. The buffer can be drawn down only under systemic or idiosyncratic stress, not to compete in normal times.
facts.locator: Paragraphs 250 and 251, Table 46; S03 printed pp. 352-354, section 13.14

facts.statement: The Basel III leverage ratio is the capital measure divided by the exposure measure, expressed as a percentage; the capital measure is Tier 1 capital. Under the Reserve Bank's Directions the minimum leverage ratio is 4 per cent for a domestic systemically important bank (D-SIB) and 3.5 per cent for other banks; the capital measure, exposure measure and ratio are disclosed at quarter-end, and the minimum must be met at all times. The courseware adds that the Basel Committee tested 3 per cent, that the Reserve Bank initially fixed 4.5 per cent and relaxed it by a circular of 6 June 2019, and that leverage ratio is one of the four indicators in the prompt corrective action framework. The leverage ratio is meant to constrain build-up of leverage in the banking sector and to back the risk-based requirements with a simple, non-risk-based backstop.
facts.locator: Paragraphs 262 to 264; S03 printed p. 354, section 13.15

facts.statement: The countercyclical capital buffer (CCCB) is held in CET1 only and may vary from 0 to 2.5 per cent of risk-weighted assets depending on the Reserve Bank's assessment; its aims are to build a buffer in good times that can be used to maintain credit flow in difficult times and to restrict indiscriminate lending in periods of excess credit growth. The decision is normally pre-announced with a lead time of four quarters. The credit-to-GDP gap (the difference between the credit-to-GDP ratio and its long-term trend) is the main indicator, used with gross NPA growth, and supplementary indicators include the incremental credit-deposit ratio over three years, an industry outlook assessment index and the interest coverage ratio. The lower threshold at which the buffer is activated is a credit-to-GDP gap of 3 percentage points; the upper threshold at which it reaches the maximum of 2.5 per cent is 15 percentage points; in between it rises gradually from 0 to 2.5 per cent. A bank that does not meet the CCCB is subject to restrictions on discretionary distributions as an extension of the CCB; with both buffers at 2.5 per cent the CET1 bands for the conservation ratios widen in steps of 25 per cent of the combined requirement (5 per cent). The courseware says the Reserve Bank has not required the CCCB to be maintained (0 per cent) since proposing it in 2015.
facts.locator: Paragraphs 258 and 259; S03 printed pp. 354-356, section 13.16

facts.statement: Under the Reserve Bank's framework for domestic systemically important banks (22 July 2014), identification is a two-step process: the Reserve Bank decides the sample of banks, then computes a composite score of systemic importance from indicators of size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity; it identifies and discloses D-SIBs annually and places them in buckets, each with an additional CET1 requirement as a percentage of risk-weighted assets: bucket 5 1.00 per cent, bucket 4 0.80, bucket 3 0.60, bucket 2 0.40, bucket 1 0.20. The surcharge applies at solo and consolidated levels and as an extension of the CCB; a D-SIB in bucket 1 must hold CET1 of 8.2 per cent to avoid distribution restrictions. D-SIBs also face differentiated supervision. A foreign bank that is a G-SIB maintains a surcharge in India proportionate to its Indian risk-weighted assets, and one that is a D-SIB in India maintains the D-SIB surcharge. The assessment methodology was reviewed in December 2023. The courseware lists State Bank of India (bucket 3), ICICI Bank (bucket 1) and HDFC Bank (bucket 1) on the basis of March 2018 data; the current list was not retrieved.
facts.locator: Paragraphs 253 to 257 and Table 47; S03 printed pp. 356-358, section 13.17

facts.statement: Risk based supervision (RBS), as the courseware describes it, moved the Reserve Bank from the transaction-centric CAMELS and CALCS approaches to a risk based approach, following the report of a high level steering committee chaired by the Deputy Governor, Dr K. C. Chakrabarty. Its supervisory approach aims at protecting depositors and promoting financial stability, with a single point of contact (Supervisory Relationship Manager) in the Department of Banking Supervision, off-site and on-site tools with on-site intensity set by the level of risk and the probable impact of failure, and a six-step process: understanding the bank (bank profile), risk assessment (risk matrix), planning of supervisory activities, defining examination activities, inspection procedure, and reporting findings and follow-up. Stress testing, reverse stress testing and thematic reviews support it. Supervisory ratings measure the riskiness of a bank and are confidential: A good (probability of failure well below the risk appetite), B satisfactory, C unsatisfactory (marginally higher probability of failure), D poor (would need to raise capital and restructure), E very poor (no longer viable; to be wound up or merged). Governance assessment covers competence, strategies and policies, internal control and audit, internal risk management structure, conflict of interest policy and transparency, and segregation of the posts of Chairman and CEO.

payload.title: Pillar 2: the supervisory review and the ICAAP
payload.core_explanation_md:
**SREP** (supervisory review and evaluation) and the bank's **ICAAP** (internal capital adequacy assessment process) ensure the bank has **capital for all its risks**, not just the three in Pillar 1.

**What it addresses**: risks **not fully captured** by the Pillar 1 minimum, risks **not captured at all**, and **external factors**. Examples: **interest rate risk in the banking book, credit concentration, liquidity, settlement, reputational, strategic risk, model risk, weak mitigants, residual securitisation risk**.

**The four Basel principles**
| # | Who | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Bank** | assess **capital against its risk profile** and have a **capital strategy** |
| **2** | **Supervisor** | **review** the ICAAP; **act** if not satisfied |
| **3** | **Bank / supervisor** | **operate above the minimum**; supervisor may **require more** |
| **4** | **Supervisor** | **intervene early**; **rapid remedial action** |

**ICAAP**: **forward-looking**, **risk-based**, with **stress tests and scenarios**, **independently reviewed**; any **model** needs **documentation, back testing, independent validation, stress testing**.

payload.title: Pillar 3: market discipline through disclosure
payload.core_explanation_md:
Pillar 3 lets **market participants** judge a bank's **scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment processes and capital adequacy**.

- **Level**: **top consolidated entity** of the group; an individual bank discloses **stand-alone** when it is **not** the top entity.
- **Frequency**: **at least half yearly**, audited or not; **quarterly** for **DF-2 (capital adequacy)**, **DF-3 (credit risk, general)** and **DF-4 (credit risk, standardised approach)**.
- **Where**: in published results, or at least **on the bank's website** (a **regulatory disclosures section**; the courseware adds a **three-year archive**).
- The **main features of capital instruments** template is updated **whenever an instrument is issued, redeemed, converted or written down**.

payload.title: The capital conservation buffer and the distribution limits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**CCB**: **2.5% of RWA in CET1**, **above the minimum**, built in **good times**, drawn in **stress**.

**What is restricted**: **only distributions** (dividends, buybacks, **discretionary payments on other Tier 1 instruments**, **discretionary staff bonuses**), **not business operations**.

| CET1 ratio (after current retained earnings) | Share of earnings that must be conserved |
| --- | --- |
| **5.5% – 6.125%** | **100%** |
| **> 6.125% – 6.75%** | **80%** |
| **> 6.75% – 7.375%** | **60%** |
| **> 7.375% – 8.0%** | **40%** |
| **> 8.0%** | **0%** |

- CET1 is used **first** to meet the **5.5% CET1, 7% Tier 1 and 9% total** minima, so **9% CET1 with no AT1 or Tier 2 = zero buffer** and a **100% constraint**.
- **No positive earnings and CET1 below 8%**: **no positive net distributions**.
- The buffer may be used **only in systemic or bank-specific stress**, **not to compete** in normal times.

payload.title: The leverage ratio
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Leverage ratio = capital measure (Tier 1) ÷ exposure measure**, in %.

**Minimum in India**: **4% for D-SIBs**, **3.5% for other banks**; **met at all times**; **disclosed at quarter-end**.

**Purpose**: stop **build-up of leverage** that forces destabilising **deleveraging**, and give a **simple, non-risk-based backstop** to the risk-based ratios.

**Courseware history**: BCBS tested **3%**; RBI first set **4.5%**, relaxed it by a circular of **6 June 2019**; the ratio is one of the **four prompt corrective action indicators**.

payload.title: The countercyclical capital buffer
payload.core_explanation_md:
**CCCB**: **CET1 only**, **0 to 2.5% of RWA**, set by RBI.

**Aims**: build **capital in good times** to keep **credit flowing in bad times**, and **curb excess credit growth**.

- **Announced** normally **four quarters ahead**.
- **Main indicator**: **credit-to-GDP gap** (credit-to-GDP ratio minus its long-term trend), read with **gross NPA growth**; other indicators: **incremental credit-deposit ratio over three years**, **industry outlook index**, **interest coverage ratio**.
- **Lower threshold 3 percentage points** (buffer starts); **upper threshold 15 points** (buffer at **2.5%**, until RBI signals withdrawal); **in between it rises gradually from 0 to 2.5%**.
- A bank short of the CCCB faces **restrictions on discretionary distributions**, as an **extension of the CCB**.
- With **CCB 2.5% and CCCB 2.5%**, the **CET1 bands widen** to steps of **25% of 5%** (1.25 points): **5.5–6.75: 100%; 6.75–8.0: 80%; 8.0–9.25: 60%; 9.25–10.5: 40%; above 10.5: 0%**.
- The courseware says RBI has **not required** the CCCB (0%) since proposing it in **2015**.

payload.title: Domestic systemically important banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**D-SIB framework** (RBI, **22 July 2014**): a **two-step** process: RBI picks a **sample of banks**, then computes a **composite score** from **size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity**; D-SIBs are **identified and disclosed every year** and put into **buckets**.

| Bucket | Additional CET1 (% of RWA) |
| --- | --- |
| **5** | **1.00** |
| **4** | **0.80** |
| **3** | **0.60** |
| **2** | **0.40** |
| **1** | **0.20** |

- Applies at **solo and consolidated** level and **as an extension of the CCB**: a **bucket 1** D-SIB needs **CET1 of 8.2%** (5.5 + 2.5 + 0.2) to avoid distribution limits.
- Also **differentiated supervision**.
- **Foreign banks**: a **G-SIB** keeps a surcharge in India **in proportion to its Indian RWA**; a **D-SIB in India** keeps the D-SIB surcharge.
- Methodology **reviewed December 2023**. The courseware's list (**SBI bucket 3; ICICI and HDFC bucket 1**) uses **March 2018 data** and is not the current list.

payload.title: Risk based supervision
payload.core_explanation_md:
**From** the transaction-centric **CAMELS / CALCS** approaches **to risk based supervision** (RBS), after a **high level steering committee** chaired by Deputy Governor **Dr K. C. Chakrabarty**.

- **Aim**: **protect depositors** and **promote financial stability**; a **Supervisory Relationship Manager** is the **single point of contact**.
- **Intensity** of on-site work follows the **level of risk** and the **probable impact of failure**, not business volume.
- **Six steps**: **bank profile → risk assessment (matrix) → planning supervisory activities → defining examination activities → inspection procedure → reporting and follow-up**.
- **Tools**: **stress and reverse stress testing**, **thematic reviews**.

**Supervisory rating** (confidential; measures **riskiness**): **A** good; **B** satisfactory; **C** unsatisfactory; **D** poor (**raise capital and restructure**); **E** very poor (**wind up or merge**).

**Governance** reviewed on: **competence, strategies and policies, internal control and audit, risk management structure, conflict of interest policy, transparency**, and **separate Chairman and CEO**.

payload.title: How much of the earnings may a bank pay out?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank's CET1 ratio after including current retained earnings is 7.0% and its distributable earnings are ₹800 crore. What share of earnings must it conserve and how much may it pay as dividends, buybacks and discretionary bonuses?

worked_steps.description: Find the band: 7.0% lies above 6.75% and up to 7.375%.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The bank must conserve 60% (₹480 crore) and may distribute at most ₹320 crore

self_check.prompt_text: What would happen to the limit if the CET1 ratio rose to 8.2%?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It would be above 8.0%, so no conservation is required and the capital conservation constraint falls away.

payload.title: CET1 needed by a D-SIB to avoid distribution limits
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a D-SIB in bucket 2 has risk-weighted assets of ₹2,50,000 crore. Find the CET1 ratio and amount it needs to avoid distribution restrictions.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: The bank needs a CET1 ratio of 8.4%, which is ₹21,000 crore

self_check.prompt_text: What is the same figure for a bucket 5 D-SIB?

payload.title: Testing the leverage ratio
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has Tier 1 capital of ₹9,000 crore and an exposure measure of ₹2,40,000 crore. Find its leverage ratio and test it against the minimum for an ordinary bank and for a D-SIB.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: The ratio is 3.75%: enough for an ordinary bank but short of the 4% required of a D-SIB

self_check.prompt_text: How much more Tier 1 capital would a D-SIB need, holding exposure fixed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 4% of 2,40,000 is ₹9,600 crore, so ₹600 crore more.

items.title: Pillar 2: the supervisory review and the ICAAP
items.core_explanation_md:
**SREP** (supervisory review and evaluation) and the bank's **ICAAP** (internal capital adequacy assessment process) ensure the bank has **capital for all its risks**, not just the three in Pillar 1.

**What it addresses**: risks **not fully captured** by the Pillar 1 minimum, risks **not captured at all**, and **external factors**. Examples: **interest rate risk in the banking book, credit concentration, liquidity, settlement, reputational, strategic risk, model risk, weak mitigants, residual securitisation risk**.

**The four Basel principles**
| # | Who | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Bank** | assess **capital against its risk profile** and have a **capital strategy** |
| **2** | **Supervisor** | **review** the ICAAP; **act** if not satisfied |
| **3** | **Bank / supervisor** | **operate above the minimum**; supervisor may **require more** |
| **4** | **Supervisor** | **intervene early**; **rapid remedial action** |

**ICAAP**: **forward-looking**, **risk-based**, with **stress tests and scenarios**, **independently reviewed**; any **model** needs **documentation, back testing, independent validation, stress testing**.

items.title: Pillar 3: market discipline through disclosure
items.core_explanation_md:
Pillar 3 lets **market participants** judge a bank's **scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment processes and capital adequacy**.

- **Level**: **top consolidated entity** of the group; an individual bank discloses **stand-alone** when it is **not** the top entity.
- **Frequency**: **at least half yearly**, audited or not; **quarterly** for **DF-2 (capital adequacy)**, **DF-3 (credit risk, general)** and **DF-4 (credit risk, standardised approach)**.
- **Where**: in published results, or at least **on the bank's website** (a **regulatory disclosures section**; the courseware adds a **three-year archive**).
- The **main features of capital instruments** template is updated **whenever an instrument is issued, redeemed, converted or written down**.

items.title: The capital conservation buffer and the distribution limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**CCB**: **2.5% of RWA in CET1**, **above the minimum**, built in **good times**, drawn in **stress**.

**What is restricted**: **only distributions** (dividends, buybacks, **discretionary payments on other Tier 1 instruments**, **discretionary staff bonuses**), **not business operations**.

| CET1 ratio (after current retained earnings) | Share of earnings that must be conserved |
| --- | --- |
| **5.5% – 6.125%** | **100%** |
| **> 6.125% – 6.75%** | **80%** |
| **> 6.75% – 7.375%** | **60%** |
| **> 7.375% – 8.0%** | **40%** |
| **> 8.0%** | **0%** |

- CET1 is used **first** to meet the **5.5% CET1, 7% Tier 1 and 9% total** minima, so **9% CET1 with no AT1 or Tier 2 = zero buffer** and a **100% constraint**.
- **No positive earnings and CET1 below 8%**: **no positive net distributions**.
- The buffer may be used **only in systemic or bank-specific stress**, **not to compete** in normal times.

items.title: The leverage ratio
items.core_explanation_md:
**Leverage ratio = capital measure (Tier 1) ÷ exposure measure**, in %.

**Minimum in India**: **4% for D-SIBs**, **3.5% for other banks**; **met at all times**; **disclosed at quarter-end**.

**Purpose**: stop **build-up of leverage** that forces destabilising **deleveraging**, and give a **simple, non-risk-based backstop** to the risk-based ratios.

**Courseware history**: BCBS tested **3%**; RBI first set **4.5%**, relaxed it by a circular of **6 June 2019**; the ratio is one of the **four prompt corrective action indicators**.

items.title: The countercyclical capital buffer
items.core_explanation_md:
**CCCB**: **CET1 only**, **0 to 2.5% of RWA**, set by RBI.

**Aims**: build **capital in good times** to keep **credit flowing in bad times**, and **curb excess credit growth**.

- **Announced** normally **four quarters ahead**.
- **Main indicator**: **credit-to-GDP gap** (credit-to-GDP ratio minus its long-term trend), read with **gross NPA growth**; other indicators: **incremental credit-deposit ratio over three years**, **industry outlook index**, **interest coverage ratio**.
- **Lower threshold 3 percentage points** (buffer starts); **upper threshold 15 points** (buffer at **2.5%**, until RBI signals withdrawal); **in between it rises gradually from 0 to 2.5%**.
- A bank short of the CCCB faces **restrictions on discretionary distributions**, as an **extension of the CCB**.
- With **CCB 2.5% and CCCB 2.5%**, the **CET1 bands widen** to steps of **25% of 5%** (1.25 points): **5.5–6.75: 100%; 6.75–8.0: 80%; 8.0–9.25: 60%; 9.25–10.5: 40%; above 10.5: 0%**.
- The courseware says RBI has **not required** the CCCB (0%) since proposing it in **2015**.

items.title: Domestic systemically important banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**D-SIB framework** (RBI, **22 July 2014**): a **two-step** process: RBI picks a **sample of banks**, then computes a **composite score** from **size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity**; D-SIBs are **identified and disclosed every year** and put into **buckets**.

| Bucket | Additional CET1 (% of RWA) |
| --- | --- |
| **5** | **1.00** |
| **4** | **0.80** |
| **3** | **0.60** |
| **2** | **0.40** |
| **1** | **0.20** |

- Applies at **solo and consolidated** level and **as an extension of the CCB**: a **bucket 1** D-SIB needs **CET1 of 8.2%** (5.5 + 2.5 + 0.2) to avoid distribution limits.
- Also **differentiated supervision**.
- **Foreign banks**: a **G-SIB** keeps a surcharge in India **in proportion to its Indian RWA**; a **D-SIB in India** keeps the D-SIB surcharge.
- Methodology **reviewed December 2023**. The courseware's list (**SBI bucket 3; ICICI and HDFC bucket 1**) uses **March 2018 data** and is not the current list.

items.title: Risk based supervision
items.core_explanation_md:
**From** the transaction-centric **CAMELS / CALCS** approaches **to risk based supervision** (RBS), after a **high level steering committee** chaired by Deputy Governor **Dr K. C. Chakrabarty**.

- **Aim**: **protect depositors** and **promote financial stability**; a **Supervisory Relationship Manager** is the **single point of contact**.
- **Intensity** of on-site work follows the **level of risk** and the **probable impact of failure**, not business volume.
- **Six steps**: **bank profile → risk assessment (matrix) → planning supervisory activities → defining examination activities → inspection procedure → reporting and follow-up**.
- **Tools**: **stress and reverse stress testing**, **thematic reviews**.

**Supervisory rating** (confidential; measures **riskiness**): **A** good; **B** satisfactory; **C** unsatisfactory; **D** poor (**raise capital and restructure**); **E** very poor (**wind up or merge**).

**Governance** reviewed on: **competence, strategies and policies, internal control and audit, risk management structure, conflict of interest policy, transparency**, and **separate Chairman and CEO**.

items.title: How much of the earnings may a bank pay out?
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank's CET1 ratio after including current retained earnings is 7.0% and its distributable earnings are ₹800 crore. What share of earnings must it conserve and how much may it pay as dividends, buybacks and discretionary bonuses?

worked_steps.description: Find the band: 7.0% lies above 6.75% and up to 7.375%.

items.final_answer_with_unit: The bank must conserve 60% (₹480 crore) and may distribute at most ₹320 crore

self_check.prompt_text: What would happen to the limit if the CET1 ratio rose to 8.2%?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It would be above 8.0%, so no conservation is required and the capital conservation constraint falls away.

items.stem_md: A bank has CET1 of 6.4% (after retained earnings) and distributable earnings of ₹500 crore. What is the largest total of dividends, buybacks and bonuses it may pay, in ₹ crore?
items.correct_explanation_md: 6.4% is above 6.125% and up to 6.75%, so 80% of earnings must be conserved; it may distribute 20% of 500 = 100.

items.stem_md: With a capital conservation buffer of 2.5% and a countercyclical buffer of 1%, the courseware adds 0.625% and 0.25% per band to the minimum CET1 of 5.5%. What CET1 ratio, in per cent, lies at the top of the 100% conservation band?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 3 decimal places.

items.correct_explanation_md: Top of the first band = 5.5 + 0.625 + 0.25 = 6.375%.
